articles.title: Mock NBA Expansion Draft for New Las Vegas and Seattle Teams
articles.summary: Las Vegas and Seattle are reportedly moving closer to getting NBA expansion teams.
articles.body:
Las Vegas and Seattle are reportedly moving closer to getting NBA expansion teams.

On Tuesday, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that the process for gathering bids for an expansion team in Las Vegas "has moved with more pace than Seattle, but those Seattle conversations are continuing as well."

Charania added that "the league has been targeting as soon as the 2028-29 season for the start of these expansion teams." We weren't patient enough to wait.

B/R NBA Analysts Dan Favale and Grant Hughes have already decided which players each team would protect from an expansion draft if one were being held today. Using that pool of available players, they held their own mock expansion draft for the Vegas and Seattle teams.

A few rules of note before we get underway:

Expansion teams have only 66⅔ percent of the usual salary cap in their first year of existence. Since the 2026-27 cap is $164,961,000, our expansion teams were limited to a $109,974,000 salary cap.

Each team had to select at least 14 players.

Existing teams can lose only one player in an expansion draft. So, if Las Vegas selects a player from the OKC Thunder, Seattle cannot take one from OKC, etc.

Will any team spend 40-50 percent of their cap space on the likes of Paul George, Joel Embiid, Ja Morant or Zach LaVine? Which current teams managed to make it through the expansion draft unscathed?

Let's see how the new Las Vegas Vipers and Seattle SuperSonicBooms fill out their rosters while staying under the salary cap.

Keep scrolling to explore the entire draft.

1. Las Vegas Vipers: Jared McCain, Oklahoma City Thunder

Jared McCain isn't just unusual among the players in this pool. He might be unique.

While putting together different mock roster builds before the draft, McCain kept ending up on my team because he ticked boxes no one else did.

Young at 22, very cheap at $4.4 million and already a scorer who'd proved himself against a great defense on a postseason stage, McCain became a player and a value whom I decided the Vipers couldn't live without.

Slotting him into a prominent role meant my team would need defensive help up and down the roster, but I figured I could find that later. McCain's low-cost scoring chops and upside were too good to pass on.

The other key factor here: Taking McCain eliminated the rest of the Oklahoma City Thunder's players from the pool. Jaylin Williams and a handful of others could have helped Dan's team, but now they're unavailable. Gamesmanship!

2. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Ty Jerome, Memphis Grizzlies

The SuperSonicBooms always planned to take someone with our first pick who could run the offense without a bank-breaking salary. Owed under $10 million this coming season, Ty Jerome topped our big board.

Last year's 15-game sample size would be a red flag if he hadn't just finished third in Sixth Man of the Year voting during the 2024-25 campaign. That allows us to place genuine stock in Jerome grading out as one of the league's most efficient self-created shot-makers in his brief time with Memphis.

Even if he tapers off a bit, the 29-year-old is a viable floor spacer, reasonable half-court initiator and push-shot extraordinaire. Landing someone like him for under 8.5 percent of our salary cap is a friggin' coup—both on the court and as a potential trade asset down the line.

3. Las Vegas Vipers: Josh Giddey, Chicago Bulls

For most of the pre-draft run-up, I thought I was going to take Josh Giddey with my first pick. That was a weird place to be.

I'm not the biggest Giddey fan around. I think his defensive warts and shaky pull-up shooting limit his effectiveness, but there aren't any perfect players in the draft pool. There certainly aren't any others who racked up 17.0 points, 9.1 assists and 8.3 rebounds per game in 2025-26.

Giddey is a five-year vet heading into only his age-24 season. He's perhaps the only available player whose passing occasionally rubs up against the "makes everybody better" level of offensive transformation. He's certainly not Tyrese Haliburton in that regard, but Giddey also costs just $25 million. I can afford that after spending just $4.4 million on McCain.

Downside: Perimeter defense and rim protection just became even bigger issues for the Vipers.

4. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Mitchell Robinson, Boston Celtics

Our search for a defensive anchor in the middle was going to wait another pick or two. The Vipers' decision to open the draft by taking two major defensive liabilities forced our hand. They'll surely snag a big man with their next selection.

Mitchell Robinson's three-year, $47.4 million deal is a slight overpay relative to his injury history and how he must be managed moving forward. Playing him in back-to-backs is probably a no-go. He's not someone who should routinely (if ever) log 25-plus minutes a game.

Still, Robinson's offensive rebounding is generational , and he's gotten better at grabbing those misses and throwing them to shooters. We can't put a price on these second-chance opportunities when we're building a squad from other teams' spare parts.

Though Robinson's defensive malleability has slipped a tad, he remains more mobile than most other behemoths. That gives us the flexibility to run him alongside a floor-spacer with center-like size if the opportunity presents itself.

Also notable: Our own selection of Jerome removes Isaiah Stewart from consideration. That increases the urgency behind tapping the "capable center" button now.

5. Las Vegas Vipers: Marcus Smart, Houston Rockets

I don't know if this was the best pick of the draft, but it was definitely my favorite. While Marcus Smart's playmaking and defensive versatility add key dimensions to my team, the real appeal of getting him at No. 5 was Dan's deeply anguished reaction when I selected the 12-year vet.

Sometimes, making a good pick is really just about hurting your competitor. Smart, a known agitator who looks for edges wherever he can find them, would probably agree.

Though Smart's shooting comes and goes, he's always willing to fire from deep. Combined with his postseason experience, veteran savvy, rugged defensive work and capable facilitation, he's an ideal fit next to Jared McCain and Josh Giddey. He'll guard who they can't, keep the ball moving and generate extra possessions with his unmatched grifting talents.

This team is starting to get pretty interesting.

6. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Rasheer Fleming, Phoenix Suns

So much for the Vipers grabbing a big man. Las Vegas President of Curiously Carried Out Basketball Operations Grant Hughes is apparently building a team of all guards.

Are we just salty because they scooped us on Marcus Smart? Most definitely. But Rasheer Fleming was next on our board.

The selection might evoke laughter. Let it. Fleming is just 22, and at 6'9", he can play either forward spot. His 34.6 percent clip from distance as a rookie is high enough to suggest it can improve with more volume. He's among the league's feistiest offensive-rebounding combo wings.

This still rates as a dice roll, but Fleming's contract is worth the gamble. We just snared a rotation player making under 2 percent of our Year 1 salary cap. He's under team control through 2028-29.

7. Las Vegas Vipers: Allen Graves, Toronto Raptors

Allen Graves went to Santa Clara. Many years before that, I also went to Santa Clara. I'm not sure we needed to disclose that, but it might help some of you understand how he landed on the Vipers as their presumed starting power forward.

Don't worry, homerism isn't the only justification for this pick.

Graves went to the Toronto Raptors at No. 19 in the 2026 NBA draft after establishing himself as an analytics darling in college. The 6'9" forward excels at the little things, is wildly disruptive on defense and shot 41.3 percent from deep as a Bronco.

As The Athletic's Sam Vecenie wrote, "He gets steals. He rebounds, creates second chances and doesn't turn the ball over."

Though Graves doesn't project to be an elite NBA athlete, his hustle, smarts and size should allow him to make an impact on both ends. In a league increasingly obsessed with winning the possession game through offensive boards and turnover generation on D, the 20-year-old has an in-demand skill set. With a rookie-scale deal on top of all that? Yes, please.

Between him and Smart, we've got more glue guys than an Elmer's factory.

8. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Micah Potter, Portland Trail Blazers

The hunt for premium bargains continues.

Micah Potter is earning $2.8 million next season, which works out to under 2.6 percent of our salary cap. He also just drilled more than 42 percent of his triples with the Indiana Pacers on nearly seven attempts per 36 minutes. Some of these makes were absolutely filthy, too .

While Potter won't elevate our defense beyond adding size on the glass, the stretch element will be hyper-useful in five-out lineups and let us contemplate using him in tandem with Mitchell Robinson.

As an added bonus, going with him also means the Vipers, who have yet to take a true rotation big, cannot steal him for themselves.

9. Las Vegas Vipers: Jose Alvarado, New York Knicks

The draft started to get tricky right around here, as my Josh Giddey pick suddenly meant that cost-consciousness was a major factor in every choice going forward. Or, at least that's how I'm explaining my decision to take Jose Alvarado with my fifth overall pick when I still don't have a big man.

Alvarado's high-energy, on-ball defense and general chutzpah are all valuable characteristics. He adds another point guard to the mix for me. Between him and Smart, the Vipers are already locked in as the most irritating team in expansion-franchise history.

Were those intangibles worth spending my fifth pick on? Did we need to add a player who is no more than a fourth guard on this team? Can the locker-room gains and spark-plug impact matter that much, especially when the roster is still short a center?

10. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: De'Anthony Melton, Golden State Warriors

Ty Jerome needs bodies in the backcourt who can help insulate him against the toughest (and quickest) defensive assignments. With the Vipers hoarding guards, now feels like a necessary time to check that box.

De'Anthony Melton has a perpetually checkered health bill and shot under 30 percent from three last season, but he retains his flair for defensive disruption. If he can regain the touch he parlayed into a 38.3 percent clip on triples in the previous four seasons, having him on a mini-mid-level salary is a coup for the SuperSonicBooms.

Now, if Melton's outside shot is cooked, we'll have some difficult decisions to make. Expect us to be on the prowl for more dependable spacers in upcoming picks to increase our optionality beside Jerome.

11. Las Vegas Vipers: Sion James, Charlotte Hornets

Sion James puts a meager $2.4 million hit on our cap, a bargain price for someone who appeared in all 82 games as a rookie. James is a pure three-and-D wing, destined to take over for Lu Dort as "the player most likely to have a second career as an inside linebacker" whenever that mantle is passed on.

Between Marcus Smart, Jose Alvarado and now James, the Vipers have a growing collection of players who are absolute nightmares for opposing scorers. These are the kinds of balancing moves you need to make when you build your backcourt initially around Josh Giddey and Jared McCain.

Imagine all the tricks Smart and Alvarado will teach James, whose physicality and lateral quickness already make him one of the best young on-ball defenders around.

12. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Ziaire Williams, Los Angeles Lakers

Ziaire Williams is one of the best three-and-D options on the expansion-draft board, period. That might say more about the overall pool of available players. There are the breaks when you're building your team from the ground up using other squads' castoffs.

Also, Williams gets grabbed during this process anyway, even if higher-end options are on the table. Minimum contracts are catnip for franchises with budgets as tight as ours.

Standing 6'9", the 24-year-old guarded up-and-down the positional spectrum during his past two seasons on the Brooklyn Nets. Although he won't help us on the glass, his defensive playmaking has improved, as has his overall strength level, making it easier to stick him on bigger, burlier forwards if we deem it necessary.

Question marks abound on the offensive end, where Williams shouldn't dribble unless absolutely forced to, despite his impulses to the contrary. That'll require us to maximize his time alongside Ty Jerome—or ensure we lasso in other ball-handling options to stash around him.

This is doable. After Williams hit 38 and 35 percent of his arc threes in each of the past two years, respectively, the hope is that he can nudge up his efficiency and volume from the corners going forward.

13. Las Vegas Vipers: Isaiah Collier, Utah Jazz

Isaiah Collier is 21 and already does a couple of things extremely well: getting to the rim and setting up his teammates.

He ranked in the 88th percentile in assist percentage at his position last year and finished with a 74.0 percent clip near the basket. The Vipers already have a handful of guards, but none of them tick the boxes that Collier does.

As a shooter and defender, the two-year pro has a ton to work on. Collier has what amounts to a first-option starter kit and could develop into a pretty interesting player in his third season if he addresses some of his shortcomings. For $2.8 million in salary, it's worth betting that a guy who was regarded as the No. 1 overall player in the 2023 recruiting class has a leap in him.

If it seems like we're getting a little too conservative in our spending by targeting two straight minimum-salary players, you should know something about vipers (and Vipers). Both the snake and the team are very patient. They'll bide their time, sitting still for hours until the right opportunity to strike presents itself, at which point they move with great speed and purpose.

14. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Duncan Robinson, Detroit Pistons

Are we having a competition to see who can stockpile the most guards in the top half of this draft? I'm asking for the Vipers, whose selection of Isaiah Collier doesn't pass the sniff test.

At any rate, here is that deadeye shooting we promised—and desperately need.

Duncan Robinson will take his licks defensively against certain matchups, but we can't pass up the chance to add his career 39.9 percent long-range clip, which comes on over seven attempts per game. He's not a stationary spacer, either. Robinson pressures opponents with his movement and has even improved his inside-the-arc decision-making and passing connectivity over the past three seasons.

Taking on his $16 million salary isn't ideal. Then again, we have money to burn with this pick—and, quite frankly, our future ones. Robinson's expiring contract also comes in handy if, as we march toward a title in Year 1 of our existence, we decide to take a swing on the midseason trade market.

15. Las Vegas Vipers: Myles Turner, Milwaukee Bucks

Myles Turner is the most expensive player either team has selected so far, but his $26.6 million doesn't wreck the Vipers' books because of all the dirt-cheap picks we've made to this point. Plus, his ability to space the floor at center while still protecting the rim fits perfectly into the gaps on the roster.

Now, if Josh Giddey or Jared McCain's matchup gets loose, he'll just run into Turner at the basket. If we don't get the shooting we're hoping for from Allen Graves, Marcus Smart, Sion James or anyone else, we've got the cheat code with a floor-stretching big man to ensure good spacing.

Turner is only 30, has Finals experience (don't ask how he played in that series) and is being dramatically undervalued because he joined everyone else who played for the Milwaukee Bucks last year in having a forgotten season. Even toiling in obscurity, he put up 15.9 points, 7.1 rebounds and 2.2 blocks per 36 minutes while drilling 38.3 percent of his threes.

For this team, Turner is a premium asset who justifies the premium price. Also, Dan took Mitchell Robinson several rounds ago, and I panicked.

16. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Bub Carrington, Washington Wizards

With our expansion-draft counterpart finally taking an (overly expensive) center, it's time for us to fill another hole: secondary ball-handling.

Catch-all metrics don't tend to love Bub Carrington. That can happen when you're one of the primary engines of the tanking rebuilding Washington Wizards for the first two years of your career.

Carrington can throw some truly awful passes for someone who doesn't attack at warp speed. It's pretty clear he won't ever consistently get two feet in the paint or draw fouls. His shooting has quietly improved at a reasonable volume, as he's a viable caretaker for second units.

Given his 40.3 percent clip on threes last season, positional size and familiarity working off others in Washington, we also envision him getting reps next to Ty Jerome, while we backstop the two of them with Mitchell Robinson and a combination of our rangy wing defenders.

17. Las Vegas Vipers: Jay Huff, Indiana Pacers

Wings and guards had been in short supply for a couple of rounds by this point, so I figured it made sense to take a second straight center.

Jay Huff was a per-minute star with the Memphis Grizzlies in 2024-25 and performed similarly for the Indiana Pacers in an expanded role last season. He won't be asked to start, as Turner is ahead of him on the depth chart, but Huff brings similarly valuable shooting and shot-blocking to a backup role. In theory, the team can play with the same spacing regardless of which big man is on the floor.

Huff joined Turner and Victor Wembanyama as the only players (minimum 500 minutes) to average at least 2.0 blocks and 2.0 made threes per 36 minutes in 2025-26.

At $2.7 million, the price was right, too.

18. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Mouhamed Gueye, Atlanta Hawks

Jay Huff was a cost-controlled big on our radar, so good job by the Vipers. Another cheap big on our radar? Mr. Mo Gueye.

The 23-year-old is recovering from left foot surgery, so this could be a tad bit early, especially knowing the Vipers just took back-to-back bigs.

Still, Gueye's defensive versatility and playmaking are too tantalizing to pass up.

Frontcourt mobility is paramount for a roster built around Ty Jerome. When healthy, Gueye can bring it in spades at both the 4 and 5 spots—all for the bargain price of $2.4 million.

19. Las Vegas Vipers: Brook Lopez, Los Angeles Clippers

As it turns out, waiting on big men was the right call after all.

Brook Lopez transitioned into a backup role for the first time in his career last season. He gets to take it even easier as the Vipers' third-stringer.

Still a high-volume gunner from deep who has drilled at least 36 percent of his threes in each of the last four seasons, and a reliable deterrent against paint scorers, the 38-year-old big man also adds locker-room wisdom to the mix.

He and Jose Alvarado give the Vipers two players with relatively recent championship runs.

Lopez has the heft to match up against the burlier bigs who'll be too much for Turner and Huff. Of course, he allows the Vipers to keep a spacing center on the floor at all times.

At $9 million, Lopez isn't cheap. But we're nearing the end of the draft and can't take any leftover cash with us.

20. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Justin Edwards, Philadelphia 76ers

We can already hear the boo birds. We acknowledge them. Understand them.

Justin Edwards gives us a sub-$2.5 million flier on another three-and-D wing. Yes, he declined from his rookie to sophomore season, yet he still drained 37.2 percent of his triples last year despite his role evaporating.

Better players are on the board. We admit that, but we're positioning ourselves to throw some real money around in these later rounds after amassing plenty of clearance-priced rotation swings.

21. Las Vegas Vipers: Jamal Cain, Orlando Magic

Jamal Cain is 27, shot 38.4 percent from beyond the arc in a limited role last year and might be the last player on the board whom you could credibly call a two-way wing.

He started playoff games for the Orlando Magic last season, while being a monster on the offensive glass, playing extremely hard and doing this in a game where he also capably defended Cade Cunningham:

Cain has seen action for three teams since entering the league during the 2022-23 season. He is being selected here based on a very small sample of solid play last year.

It's possible that he'll prove his shooting from last season was real while doubling down on the rim attacks and disruptive defense he flashed. Is it likely? Probably not, but we're only spending $2.6 million to find out.

22. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Bones Hyland, Minnesota Timberwolves

Upon further glances at the Vipers' roster, the SuperSonicBooms are getting uneasy about how many players can make something happen on offense with the rock in their hands.

Enter Bones Hyland, a ball-handler on the come-up, who doesn't even burn 2.6 percent of our salary cap.

Among 108 players who took as many pull-up jumpers last year, Hyland's 55.0 effective field-goal percentage ranked eighth. Bub Carrington's 55.5 effective field-goal rate ranked sixth.

Nobody in Seattle is under the impression that Hyland will help the defensive mission. That is what the many, many hybrid wings we already have are for. The on-ball jiggle and joggle he provides is worth the concession, particularly relative to the makeup of our roster.

23. Las Vegas Vipers: Keon Ellis, Brooklyn Nets

Do the Vipers really need Keon Ellis, whose post-trade play with the Cleveland Cavaliers last year never quite justified the wrath of Sacramento Kings fans who were certain he should have been playing more?

Not exactly, but all our cash is burning a hole in our pocket. It's time to spend some of it after being so careful for most of the draft. Ellis' cap hit is a relatively high $9 million.

If money is being thrown around a little more recklessly than before, it might as well go to a guy who can make life hard for opposing ball-handlers while also hitting threes at a just-good-enough clip.

Ellis is a good complement to Jared McCain, Josh Giddey and Marcus Smart, as he can work off the ball while chasing around the quicker guards those three shouldn't have to. Plus, the further removed he gets from the Kings, the better he's likely to be.

24. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Daniel Gafford, Dallas Mavericks

It's time for the SuperSonicBooms to spend some real money.

Bringing in another big who will be more available than Mitchell Robinson is non-negotiable. Micah Potter and Mo Gueye are already on the roster, but Daniel Gafford more effectively mirrors what we get from Mitch.

The 27-year-old Gafford isn't as mobile on the defensive end. Fewer possessions will be swallowed whole by opposing half-court offenses. But the baseline rim protection is more than good enough.

Among 32 players who challenged at least five close-range looks per game last year, the 55 percent finishing rate Gafford gave up was the sixth-stingiest. Career stalwarts Victor Wembanyama, Chet Holmgren, Jaren Jackson Jr., Rudy Gobert and Anthony Davis (with a small sample size) were the only names ahead of him.

What Gafford lacks in defensive dynamism beyond protecting the hoop, he makes up for with elite finishing chops he can access on a variety of catches and spots around the floor. On nights in which both he and Robinson are available, we now have one of the league's better center rotations.

25. Las Vegas Vipers: Harrison Barnes, San Antonio Spurs

With about $10.5 million left to split between two or three picks, the Vipers are making sure their culture is solid.

Harrison Barnes is an NBA champ who's earned respect for his maturity and high character wherever he's played. He may still have enough to contribute as a spacing power forward as he enters his age-34 season.

Though the San Antonio Spurs booted him from the first unit late last year, Barnes still shot 38.8 percent from deep. That wasn't nearly as impressive as his 43.3 percent hit rate from three in 82 starts the prior season, but the veteran was still a helpful contributor.

Barnes can certainly occupy that role here, where we don't feature a championship-caliber roster like the Spurs. If anything, Barnes' poise and value as a tone-setting adult in the room will matter far more on an expansion team.

By paying $8 million for Barnes, we've foreclosed the possibility of adding a 15th player in this draft and have only one minimum salary slot left. No regrets.

26. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Malik Monk, Sacramento Kings

Did we wait until our third-to-last pick to grab our leading scorer and perhaps our best on-ball option? Who's to say, really? (Yes. Yes, we did.)

Malik Monk's microwave scoring comes in a unique form. He doesn't need the ball as much as other players who fall under this archetype. Most of his most effective possessions come from putting pressure on the basket.

Nearly 10 years into his career, Monk has never ranked lower than the 80th percentile in assists per pass out of drives. Coupled with a sufficiently high 36.8 percent clip from behind the rainbow since 2021, he's equal parts dynamic and adaptable to just about any situation.

We will not take this as a license to overwork him as the primary facilitator. That will be fine for secondary lineups, but he'll preferably spend time next to Ty Jerome, thanks to our surplus of wing options.

27. Las Vegas Vipers: Marvin Bagley III, Denver Nuggets

Did you guys know that Marvin Bagley III was a statistically dominant big man at Duke?

He averaged 21.0 points and 11.1 rebounds on 61.4 percent shooting, earning several honors, including ACC Player of the Year, All-Conference and Consensus All-American.

We all know how good Luka Dončić has been as a pro, yet Bagley was selected ahead of him in the 2018 draft.

I have to admit I haven't really kept up with his career since then, but I can only assume Bagley validated his collegiate performance and draft slot by earning several All-Star and All-NBA nods. What other outcome was even possible with an amateur resumé like his?

It seems like a pretty big oversight by both Dan and me that Bagley fell all the way to the 14th round of this draft. Also, a little strange: Bagley's salary is only $2.5 million. He must have taken less so his championship-worthy roster could spend more on support pieces around him.

28. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Dru Smith, Miami Heat

The SuperSonicBooms are back to bargain shopping with our final two picks. We could reel in a more expensive player and soldier onward with 14 players, but serviceable depth is our greatest ally.

Our first order of business: taking a flier on an Erik Spoelstra favorite—a distinction that definitely factors into this decision.

At one point, Dru Smith looked like a semi-capable three-point shooter who stifled or submarined rival offenses. Last year's performance hardly proves anything, but he was working his way back from an Achilles injury.

The swiftness with which Smith returned from such a devastating setback is a desirable quality in itself. Since the Heat continued to roll him out against tougher offensive matchups in smaller doses, the limb we're stepping out on with our penultimate selection isn't as flimsy as it might seem.

The Vipers are only $333,000 below the salary cap at this point in the draft, so we cannot draft another player. We're rocking with a 14-man roster for now and can sign someone to a prorated minimum contract sometime in March.

30. Seattle SuperSonicBooms: Nae'Qwan Tomlin, Cleveland Cavaliers

Nae'Qwan Tomlin plays all-gas-no-brakes basketball. The SuperSonicBooms are thrilled to have him.

The physical tools are undeniable, especially on defense. Listed at 6'10", Tomlin is hyper-malleable. His 10 highest-volume assignments last year featured bigs, one-position forwards, wings and even a guard.

Tomlin's offense is tougher to pin down. Last year's percentages from beyond the arc and at the basket don't really line up with the most idealistic projections. The situational ball-handling he displayed at Kansas State and Memphis hasn't really translated (unless you count the most recent summer league, kinda).

Even so, it's the last pick. We're taking a stab in the dark at a 25-year-old hybrid defender whose jumper form isn't broken. Sue us.

articles.title: Landing Spots for Top 5 Unsigned NBA Free Agents
articles.summary: Restricted free agent Jalen Duren is the lone starting-caliber player still on the market, but only because he and the Detroit Pistons can't agree on the final terms of his next deal.
articles.body:
Restricted free agent Jalen Duren is the lone starting-caliber player still on the market, but only because he and the Detroit Pistons can't agree on the final terms of his next deal.

Soon, the remaining free-agent options will include journeymen, last-chance prospects and feel-good reunion stories.

Where should the likes of Ochai Agbaji, Bruce Brown, Gabe Vincent and more land ahead of the 2026-27 season? Let's check out the options and pick some destinations.

Jalen Duren and the Detroit Pistons seem to be nearing a compromise.

Per Sam Amick and Hunter Patterson of The Athletic, Detroit's offer for the restricted free agent is in the $190 million range, while Duren wants at least $200 million. That's not exactly an unbridgeable gap.

Though Duren's reps clearly leaked that he is "increasingly considering" taking his $9 million qualifying offer for le verage, all signs point to this thing resolving sooner rather than later.

Detroit is right to play hardball here. Duren flopped in the playoffs, and there's no outside market for his services. On the other hand, there's no reason for the All-NBA center to make this easy on his team.

This isn't really even a proper standoff. The Pistons know Duren won't risk hundreds of millions of dollars in guaranteed money by taking his qualifying offer, and the possibility of a sign-and-trade is now vanishingly small because every other team in the league has its books in order ahead of training camp.

Still just 26 and not far removed from a 2024-25 season in which he averaged 10.4 points while hitting 39.9 percent of his threes, Ochai Agbaji should get a chance to prove he can slot into the back end of somebody's rotation as a cheap three-and-D option.

The Los Angeles Lakers never had much chance of bringing in Peyton Watson, and Jonathan Kuminga ended up signing with the Minnesota Timberwolves. If they want to address their need for athletic, two-way wing role players, Agbaji would be a low-cost option.

Though he doesn't quite have ideal size at 6'5", the No. 14 pick in the 2022 draft has consistently posted high block and offensive rebound rates for a wing. That suggests he can make the kind of impact you'd expect from a bigger player at his position—at least in a couple of areas.

At this late stage of free agency, it probably wouldn't even take a fully guaranteed deal to get Agbaji in camp. Any team built around Luka Dončić needs as many athletic three-and-D types as it can get.

The defending champion New York Knicks would be best served by finding another cheap big man to bolster depth behind Karl-Anthony Towns at center. New addition Andre Drummond is a solid backup, but he's on a minimum deal for a reason.

It sounds as if New York is most likely to trade its way to a solution at the 5. Once it does that, attention should shift to Bruce Brown, who'd provide championship-tested two-way play on the wing.

While it's true that the Knicks must shore up the center spot, positional depth behind OG Anunoby and Mikal Bridges is also a concern.

Brown is still only 30 and is coming off something of a bounce-back season with the Denver Nuggets. The veteran guard appeared in all 82 games, shot 38.5 percent from deep, posted an offensive rebound rate in the 93rd percentile for his position and even saw an uptick in steals.

That all suggests he can still offer quality spot-up shooting and plenty of disruptive play all over the floor. Perhaps most importantly, the durability Brown showed last season indicates he could take on a fairly large role. That should matter to a Knicks team that'll need to rest its key players consistently after playing well into June.

Gabe Vincent's post-Miami Heat career wasn't anything special, but there are still a few good reasons for the 30-year-old guard and his former team to reunite.

For starters, the Heat are still light at the guard spots. Though they did well to pull in the shooting they'll need around Giannis Antetokounmpo, Davion Mitchell is the only real point guard on the roster.

Vincent has never been an every-down facilitator, peaking at 3.1 assists per game with the 2021-22 Heat. But he can still defend the position, and it doesn't hurt that head coach Erik Spoelstra and veteran star Bam Adebayo have both been "big advocates" for Vincent over the summer, per Brett Siegel on the Clutch Scoops podcast.

Miami has a 15th roster spot available but is right up against the first apron hard cap. Squeezing a veteran minimum salary into that space may be possible, and Vincent seems like the most logical choice if the Heat intend to fill out a full roster.

Cam Whitmore may be on the way out of the league, but any team with a talent deficit and little to lose should be willing to give him one more shot.

The Sacramento Kings fit that description pretty well, and they should have interest in seeing if there's something valuable still hiding inside the athletic wing who was recently waived by the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Whitmore averaged 12.3 points in only 18.7 minutes per game as a rookie with the Houston Rockets but suffered from tunnel vision and committed too many defensive lapses in his second year to earn an expanded role. Shipped to Washington last year, the 21-year-old missed the second half of the season with a diagnosed venous condition.

Injury and inexperience are big reasons Whitmoe, a prospect everyone agreed was wildly talented in the run-up to the 2023 draft, is currently unemployed.

Sacramento actually has several playable wings, led by bounce-back candidate Keegan Murray. Adding Whitmore to the mix would still be worth it. The Kings are a threat to land in the relegation zone this season and need to catch lightning in a bottle to build back their talent base.

One thing Whitmore certainly has is talent.

Stats courtesy of NBA.com , Basketball Reference and Cleaning the Glass . Salary info via Spotrac .

Grant Hughes covers the NBA for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, where he appears with Bleacher Report's Dan Favale .

articles.title: Kevin Durant Makes Cameo in Drake's 'FOMO' Short Film, Wears OVO Chain in Photo
articles.summary: During a recent livestream showcasing some of his unreleased music, Drake called in Kevin Durant for a cameo appearance.
articles.body:
During a recent livestream showcasing some of his unreleased music, Drake called in Kevin Durant for a cameo appearance.

The Houston Rockets superstar dropped in to show off an OVO chain as part of Drake's FOMO short film project.

Mock NBA Expansion Draft for Las Vegas and Seattle 🤔

Per Michael Saponara of Billboard.com, Drake debuted nine unreleased tracks on the stream that featured cameos from several people, including his mother and Durant.

Durant and Drake have a longstanding friendship dating back to at least 2012 when the NBA legend shouted out the rap star for his support during the All-Star Game in which he was named MVP after scoring 36 points.

Drake has even shouted out Durant in some of his lyrics, notably on his song "Weston Road Flows" from his 2016 album Views with the line: "Shout out to KD, we relate, we get the same attention/It's rainin' money, Oklahoma City Thunder."

Basketball has sometimes gotten in the way of their friendship. Durant and Drake exchanged words after Game 2 of the 2019 NBA Finals when Durant was playing for the Golden State Warriors against Champagne Papi's beloved Toronto Raptors.

That feud didn't last long with Durant appearing in Drake's music video for "Laugh Now Cry Later" that was released in August 2020.

articles.title: Allen Iverson Welcomes Back 76ers PA Announcer Matt Cord for LeBron James' 1st Season in New Video
articles.summary: The Philadelphia 76ers announced Wednesday that longtime public address announcer Matt Cord is returning for his 29th and final season in the fall.
articles.body:
The Philadelphia 76ers announced Wednesday that longtime public address announcer Matt Cord is returning for his 29th and final season in the fall.

Sixers legend Allen Iverson and several current Sixers stars, including Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid and VJ Edgecombe, welcomed Cord back in a video shared by the team:

Mock NBA Expansion Draft for Las Vegas and Seattle 🤔

Cord announced in March that the 2025-26 season would be his last, but he reversed course ahead of what promises to be an exciting campaign in Philly.

In a statement provided to NBC Philadelphia, Cord said, "I'm incredibly grateful for the opportunity to return to the mic as PA announcer for 76ers for one more season. Serving in this role for the past 28 years has been a dream come true, and I have been fortunate to witness so many memorable moments from the best seat in the house. This is going to be a special year, and I can't wait to be back at Xfinity Mobile Arena with you all. Let's go, 76ers!"

The 76ers were one of the NBA's busiest teams during the offseason, and they could be the most improved team in the league this coming season as well.

In addition to acquiring five-time All-Star Jaylen Brown in a trade with the Boston Celtics, the Sixers signed one of the all-time greats in LeBron James in free agency.

With a projected starting lineup of James, Brown, Maxey, Embiid and Edgecombe, the 76ers figure to be among the top teams in the Eastern Conference, and they are undoubtedly championship contenders.

Should the Sixers live up to their potential, there is a chance Cord could be on the call for the organization's first NBA Finals appearance since 2001 and first championship since 1983.

articles.title: Las grandes ligas de EE.UU. plantan cara al acoso de los apostadores
articles.standfirst: La NFL, la NBA, la MLB, la NHL y la MLS piden la expulsión de por vida de las casas de apuestas a los apostadores que amenacen o acosen a los deportistas protagonistas
articles.summary: La NFL, la NBA, la MLB, la NHL y la MLS piden la expulsión de por vida de las casas de apuestas a los apostadores que amenacen o acosen a los deportistas protagonistas
articles.body: Tolerancia cero con los apostadores violentos. Las cinco grandes ligas profesionales de Estados Unidos —NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL y MLS— han unido fuerzas con los sindicatos de sus jugadores para lanzar un mensaje rotundo: amenazar o acosar a un deportista por perder una apuesta puede acabar con una expulsión de por vida de las casas de apuestas legales. La propuesta, dirigida a los reguladores de 35 estados y del Distrito de Columbia, pretende poner freno a una escalada de violencia que ya ha traspasado todas las líneas rojas. El problema ha dejado de ser virtual. Jugadores, entrenadores, árbitros, empleados de los equipos y hasta sus familiares reciben amenazas de apostadores frustrados, tanto en redes sociales como en persona. "Con demasiada frecuencia, quienes pierden apuestas deportivas envían mensajes amenazantes y de acoso a jugadores, entrenadores y sus familias a través de las redes sociales y en persona", denuncian las ligas. Y lanzan una advertencia inequívoca: "Amenazar la seguridad de un atleta o de sus familiares por una apuesta deportiva traspasa una clara línea ética y penal, y es totalmente inaceptable». El caso de Lance McCullers estremeció al deporte estadounidense. En mayo de 2025, el entonces lanzador de los Houston Astros denunció haber recibido amenazas de "encontrar a mis hijos y asesinarlos" después de una mala actuación. La investigación policial identificó al responsable: un apostador ebrio que se encontraba en el extranjero. La frontera entre perder dinero y poner en peligro una vida había quedado definitivamente borrada. Ahora las ligas quieren que quien cruce esa frontera no vuelva a apostar legalmente. Los infractores serían incluidos en una lista negra compartida entre estados, mientras se reclama un sistema rápido para trasladar las denuncias y las pruebas a reguladores y policía. "Las amenazas y el acoso en el deporte siguen aumentando, poniendo en peligro la seguridad de los participantes y la integridad del ecosistema", señala Scott Sadin, cofundador de IC360. La industria empieza a asumir que no basta con mirar hacia otro lado. Fred VanVleet, presidente del sindicato de jugadores de la NBA, puso voz al desconcierto de quienes están en primera línea: "Somos nosotros quienes asumimos toda la responsabilidad, todo el riesgo y el peligro que conlleva la relación con el juego". Y añadió: "Fue algo que nos cayó encima de repente, y creo que todos estamos tratando de adaptarnos". El deporte estadounidense ya ha dado un paso al frente: quien convierta una apuesta en una amenaza puede quedar fuera del juego para siempre.

articles.title: Knicks Sign James Wiseman, Bruce Brown to Contracts, Updated Roster Ahead of NBA Training Camp
articles.summary: The 2026 NBA champion New York Knicks added more depth to their roster ahead of the upcoming season.
articles.body:
The 2026 NBA champion New York Knicks added more depth to their roster ahead of the upcoming season.

The Knicks announced on Wednesday that they signed veteran swingman Bruce Brown, center James Wiseman and shooting guard Ochai Agbaji to training camp contracts. Per ESPN's Shams Charania , Brown, Wiseman and Agbaji join shooting guard John Konchar and center Drew Eubanks as the new signees who will be competing for one of New York's final two open roster spots.

Per Spotrac , the Knicks are $17.9 million over the tax threshold for the 2026-27 season. After signing Brown, Wiseman and Agbaji, New York's updated roster now looks like this:

PG: Jalen Brunson; Miles McBride; Jose Alvarado; Tyler Kolek

SG: Josh Hart; Jordan Clarkson; John Konchar; Ochai Agbaji

SF: Mikal Bridges; Landry Shamet; Bruce Brown

PF: OG Anunoby; Mohamed Diawara; Pacôme Dadiet

C: Karl-Anthony Towns; Andre Drummond; Drew Eubanks; James Wiseman

ESPN's Bobby Marks reported that while New York has two open roster spots, they will only be able to keep one player if they don't make a trade. The team will be able to offer the veteran minimum of $2.4 million to whoever earns the final spot.

A one-time NBA champion with the Denver Nuggets in 2023, Brown could have the leg up on the rest of the competition. The eight-year veteran has built a reputation as a do-everything "glue guy" who can contribute in multiple ways. He played in all 82 games for the Nuggets this past season and averaged 7.9 points, 3.9 rebounds, 2.1 assists and 1.0 steals. It was the first time in the 30-year-old's career that he didn't miss a single game.

The No. 2 pick in the 2020 NBA draft, Wiseman is still trying to shed the label of one of the biggest draft busts in recent memory. He most recently played for the Indiana Pacers before being released in December, and he's appeared in a combined five games over the last two seasons.

Agbaji, Konchar and Eubanks have never averaged 10 points or more in a full season in their respective NBA careers, so they will have a lot of work to do to prove they deserve a roster spot in New York.

The Knicks retained most of their championship core from last season while adding a few new faces to improve around the margins. It can be expected that the player who earns the final roster spot will be someone who shows New York he can help the team defend its first title in 53 years.

articles.title: Knicks news: Ex-Nuggets NBA champion, Warriors draft bust among signings
articles.summary: The New York Knicks are just over a month away from kicking off their 2026 NBA title defense. The Knicks will be returning most of their championship core fr...
articles.body:
The New York Knicks are just over a month away from kicking off their 2026 NBA title defense. The Knicks will be returning most of their championship core from a year ago, although Mitchell Robinson did depart in free agency for the rival Boston Celtics , with Andre Drummond replacing him as the Knicks' backup big man.

Now, the team has brought in a former NBA champion with veteran experience ahead of training camp.

"Free agent Bruce Brown has signed a training camp contract with the New York Knicks ," reported NBA insider Shams Charania of ESPN on X, formerly Twitter.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

The Knicks also reported on X that they had signed former Golden State Warriors big man James Wiseman to a contract.

Brown won a championship with the Nuggets in 2023, playing a key role off the bench during their steamrolling of the competition in the playoffs. He then went on to sign with the Indiana Pacers and bounced around a bit before returning to the Nuggets, where he played a smaller role last season, but still provided some solid production at times.

The Knicks' depth wasn't exactly a strong point for the team last year, despite their march to the championship, although they did get some unexpected big contributions from players like Landry Shamet off the bench during their playoff run, and adding Brown to the mix would give them another contributor who can impact winning at a high level. ClutchPoints' Brett Siegel had previously mentioned the Knicks signing Brown ahead of camp as a possibility.

Later, NBA insider Marc Stein reported that the Knicks had signed another NBA vet.

"The Knicks have also just signed Ochai Agbaji ," he reported on X.

It remains to be seen how the Knicks will respond to prosperity after spending decades being the laughingstock of the NBA, but it's certainly a problem that New York fans are happy to have as the new season approaches.

articles.title: Revolución en la Liga Endesa: las nuevas faltas que cambian el baloncesto
articles.standfirst: Adiós a las antideportivas y se incorporan las disruptivas, flagrantes y dos tipos de técnicas
articles.summary: Adiós a las antideportivas y se incorporan las disruptivas, flagrantes y dos tipos de técnicas
articles.body: La Liga Endesa 2026-27 estrena nuevo vocabulario y nuevas reglas para las acciones más controvertidas del juego. La competición adapta las modificaciones introducidas por FIBA con un objetivo claro: distinguir mejor entre una falta táctica, una conducta antideportiva y una acción que pone en riesgo al rival. El gran cambio afecta a las antiguas faltas antideportivas, que desaparecen para dar paso a las faltas disruptivas y flagrantes. Las faltas disruptivas castigarán principalmente las acciones tácticas para cortar un contraataque cuando el defensor no tiene una opción real de jugar el balón, o las faltas cometidas en los últimos segundos de un cuarto para detener el reloj. Mantienen la penalización de dos tiros libres y posesión, pero tienen una diferencia importante: no computan para la descalificación por acumulación. Las faltas flagrantes, en cambio, quedan reservadas para los contactos que van mucho más allá de lo normal en el baloncesto y que son violentos o pueden provocar una lesión, haya balón de por medio o no. También se sancionan con dos tiros libres y posesión, pero aquí sí hay consecuencias disciplinarias: dos flagrantes suponen la descalificación, al igual que una flagrante combinada con una técnica de categoría 1. La otra gran novedad llega con las faltas técnicas, que ahora se separan en dos categorías. Las técnicas de categoría 1 están relacionadas con la conducta: faltas de respeto, provocaciones, burlas, lenguaje ofensivo o actitudes desafiantes hacia jugadores, entrenadores, árbitros, aficionados u otros participantes. También podrán utilizarse cuando exista un enfrentamiento entre jugadores con contacto físico que no llegue al nivel de una falta flagrante o descalificante. Sí cuentan para la descalificación por acumulación. Las técnicas de categoría 2 tienen un carácter exclusivamente administrativo y, a diferencia de las anteriores, solo pueden ser señaladas a jugadores. Entrarán aquí acciones como retrasar deliberadamente un saque, colgarse del aro sin justificación, incorporarse tarde a la pista tras un descanso o tocar el balón antes de que llegue al aro en el último tiro libre. No computan para la descalificación por acumulación. En resumen: la Liga Endesa afina el castigo para que no todas las faltas tengan el mismo peso. Una interrupción táctica ya no tendrá la misma consideración que un contacto violento, y una infracción administrativa tampoco será tratada como una conducta irrespetuosa. El baloncesto cambia las etiquetas para intentar que la sanción sea más proporcional a lo sucedido en pista.

articles.title: Kyrie Irving offers to pay fine for Texans' Azeez Al-Shaair after LB wrote on eye black in tribute to killed Palestinian girl
articles.summary: Al-Shaair was reportedly fined more than $11,000 for violation of the NFL's equipment, uniform and player appearance rules.
articles.body:
Kyrie Irving is a nine-time NBA All-Star and one-time NBA champion. He's also a vocal Palestine supporter. Irving continued to express solidarity with the country on Wednesday amid its ongoing conflict with Israel.

Al-Shaair was fined $11,941 for violating the league's equipment, uniform and player appearance rules when he displayed "Hind Rajab" in writing across his eye black during a Week 1 loss to the Buffalo Bills , according to The Athletic .

Back in 2024, Israeli forces killed Rajab, along with six members of her family, in a car that was under military fire in Gaza. She was 5 years old.

The fine Al-Shaair reportedly received is not due to his pro-Palestinian message specifically. He would have been fined for any unauthorized message written on his eye black, per NFL rules.

Under the league's equipment, uniform and player appearance guidelines, "Article 8" stipulates that "throughout the period on game day that a player is visible to the stadium and television audience (including in pregame warm-ups, in the bench area, and during postgame interviews in the locker room or on the ﬁeld), players are prohibited from wearing, displaying, or otherwise conveying personal messages either in writing or illustration, unless such message has been approved in advance by the League office."

It also reads: "Items to celebrate anniversaries or memorable events, or to honor or commemorate individuals, such as helmet decals, and arm bands and jersey patches on players' uniforms, are prohibited unless approved in advance by the League office. All such items approved by the League office, if any, must relate to team or League events or personages. The League will not grant permission for any club or player to wear, display, or otherwise convey messages, through helmet decals, arm bands, jersey patches, mouthpieces, or other items afﬁxed to game uniforms or equipment, which relate to political activities or causes, other non-football events, causes or campaigns, or charitable causes or campaigns."

Notably, Al-Shaair — a first-time Pro Bowler and the Texans' Walter Payton Man of the Year nominee last season — has previously been fined by the NFL for penning messages on his eye black.

During the 2025 campaign, he exhibited the words "stop the genocide" in a wild-card playoff win over the Pittsburgh Steelers. He was reportedly fined $11,593 for violating the aforementioned NFL rules .

He then donned the same message ahead of a divisional-round loss to the New England Patriots, although he didn't wear it during that game.

Afterward, Al-Shaair explained that he was aware that his last fine from the league was coming, but emphasized that whatever he'd have to pay didn't deter him from demonstrating his feelings.

"At the end of the day, it's bigger than me, the things that are going on," Al-Shaair said at the time . "If it makes people uncomfortable, imagine how those people feel. I think that's the biggest thing. I have no affiliation, no connection to these people other than the fact that I'm a human being. If you have a heart, then you are a human being, and you can see what's going on in the world and check yourself real quick. When I'm walking off this field, that's the type of stuff that goes through my head that I have to check myself when I'm sitting here crying about football when there's people who are dying every single day."

Irving's current profile picture on Instagram reflects his support for Palestine. It features a Palestinian child sitting with a book, as Israeli soldiers look down on him beyond a barbed-wire fence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. It was reported in April that, in the wake of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran beginning, several Palestinian children weren't able to attend school in the village of Umm al-Khair near the city of Hebron. Classes had reportedly been suspended at the start of the Iran war, and then upon their resumption, villagers said the barbed wire had been erected by Israelis, according to a report from Reuters .

Irving's profile picture update has served as a source of inspiration, including for a pair of Palestinian basketball players, as chronicled by The Athletic's Mirin Fader .

Now a point guard for the Dallas Mavericks, Irving's activism regarding the Israel-Palestine conflict goes back years .

In May 2021, he turned the focus of a news conference to the violence occurring overseas. Then playing for the Brooklyn Nets, Irving asserted , "My goal out here, my purpose, is to help humanity, and I can't sit here and not address that."

articles.title: El nuevo desafío de Saint-Supéry: "La Euroliga es la mejor liga después de la NBA”

articles.summary: El base internacional español de 20 años, ambicioso en su presentación como nuevo jugador del Valencia Basket para las próximas cuatro temporadas
articles.body: Mario Saint-Supéry ya luce como jugador del Valencia Basket. El base internacional español, de 20 años, fue presentado como nuevo jugador taronja para las próximas cuatro temporadas, después de cerrar su etapa universitaria en Gonzaga. “Muy contento de estar aquí. Creo que Valencia ahora mismo está en uno de los mejores momentos de su historia”, aseguró. El malagueño regresa a España dispuesto a dar un nuevo salto en su carrera. Tras una temporada en la NCAA en la que promedió 8,6 puntos, 3,8 asistencias y un 40% en triples, Saint-Supéry afronta ahora el reto de la Euroliga. “Aunque la NCAA es cada vez más competitiva, la Euroliga es la mejor liga del mundo después de la NBA y poder competir contra los mejores fuera de la NBA me ayudará a crecer mucho como jugador”, explicó. Valencia no es un destino cualquiera para el joven base. Además de reencontrarse con su país, su familia y sus amigos, encontró en el proyecto taronja un club con tradición de apostar por el talento nacional. “También es muy importante la historia que tiene Valencia Basket con los jugadores nacionales”, señaló, citando a jóvenes como Sergio de Larrea, Pradilla o Puerto. “Mi objetivo es ser un poco mejor cada día y Valencia Basket me puede ayudar”. Saint-Supéry llega además a un vestuario que acaba de incorporar una pieza de enorme experiencia como Nikola Mirotic. El internacional español no ocultó la trascendencia del fichaje del exNBA: “Ha jugado muchos años en la NBA y a un nivel altísimo en la Euroliga. Tenerlo en el equipo nos sube el techo a un límite inexplicable”. El primer gran desafío ya está a la vuelta de la esquina: el Barça espera este sábado en las semifinales de la Supercopa Endesa. Saint-Supéry tiene claro el camino para afrontar el estreno competitivo: “Nosotros tenemos que seguir con la misma identidad que hemos intentado mostrar esta pretemporada e ir a muerte con eso”. Un mensaje que resume la ambición con la que aterriza en Valencia. Víctor Luengo, director de Relaciones Externas del club, destacó el valor de incorporar a uno de los grandes talentos jóvenes del baloncesto español. “Es un orgullo que un talento nacional como Mario haya decidido que Valencia Basket es el sitio perfecto para continuar con su carrera. Es uno de los mejores jóvenes de nuestro país”. Cuatro años por delante y un reto mayúsculo: crecer en Valencia y hacerse un nombre entre los mejores.

LSU officials reportedly declined to engage with Ole Miss’ attorneys, directing them to the athletes, who were responsible for their own contracts. This led to disagreements as to whether the buyouts would be paid, and who would actually take care of the monetary penalties that came with them allegedly breaking their contracts. OLE MISS HAD FBI AGENT SWEEP FOOTBALL FACILITY FOR BUGS AFTER LANE KIFFIN LEFT FOR LSU Any hope that the off-field drama would cool down before Saturday’s matchup has quickly disappeared. "The University of Mississippi values its student-athletes and is committed to honoring all obligations made to them. In return, the university expects that same commitment from its student-athletes and their representatives in upholding their contracts," Ole Miss said in a statement after filing suit. "Before transferring to another institution, student-athletes Devin Harper and Princewill Umanmielen signed revenue sharing agreements that included a provision requiring them to compensate the university with a predetermined amount if they departed before fulfilling their commitment. The University of Mississippi has a responsibility to enforce its contractual terms, and this position is consistent with the actions of other institutions in the current landscape of college athletics." Via ESPN , a more detailed explanation is as follows:

The Rockets came in at No. 6 in draft assets; No. 8 in market; No. 9 in players; and No. 13 in the financial and management categories.

Regarding Houston's three-year outlook, ESPN's Zach Kram writes :

Despite a fairly underwhelming 2025-26 campaign, Houston is still in strong position for this season and beyond. Additional perspectives are available in ESPN's article . While it's certainly possible that veterans such as VanVleet, Kevin Durant , and Steven Adams could decline in productivity over the next three years due to their ages, that could be offset by continued growth from Houston's talented young core of recent first-round draft picks.

At the moment, that core features the likes of Amen Thompson , Tari Eason , Jabari Smith Jr. , Reed Sheppard , and Alperen Sengun , already a two-time NBA All-Star. As ESPN alluded to, reinforcements in future drafts are potentially on the way, as well.

articles.title: LSU to honor basketball icon Sylvia Fowles with statue on campus
articles.summary: LSU will honor basketball legend Sylvia Fowles with a statue outside the Pete Maravich Assembly Center.
articles.body:
LSU women's basketball legend Sylvia Fowles will be immortalized in bronze at her alma mater.

The university announced on Wednesday, Sept. 16, that it'll erect a statue of Fowles outside of the Pete Maravich Assembly Center in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. She will become the fifth basketball player and second woman to receive their own statue on campus, joining Bob Pettit, Shaquille O'Neil, Pete Maravich and Seimone Augustus.

LSU women's basketball head coach Kim Mulkey shared the news with Fowles during an emotional Zoom call that was shared across social media. "This is something that is extremely, extremely well earned, but baby, you're going to get a statue," Mulkey told Fowles, who laughed in disbelief at the announcement.

"It is such a privilege and an honor," an emotional Fowles added. "I definitely will not take this for granted. It says a lot to be recognized for all my hard work and I would not appreciate it the way that I do if it was not on LSU's campus. Thank you to the people who made this happen."

The two-time All-American center led the Lady Tigers to four consecutive Final Four appearances from 2004–2008. Fowles was named the 2008 Defensive Player of the Year and 2008 SEC Player of the Year, also earning first-team All-SEC honors in her final three seasons. She holds all-time LSU records for total rebounds (1570), offensive rebounds (521), blocks (321), true shooting percentage (59.4%), free throw attempts (822) and games played (144).

Fowles was elected into the LSU Athletics Hall of Fame in 2015. Her No. 34 jersey was retired two years later in 2017, joining Augustus as the only women's basketball jersey hung from the rafters inside the Maravich Center.

Now, Fowles is getting her own statue. The date for her statue reveal will be announced at a later time.

"Sylvia Fowles is one of the greatest players, not only at LSU, but in the history of our game," Mulkey said in a statement. "She is one of the most significant ambassadors that this university has and what she did for this program and LSU deserves to be recognized permanently. I am proud that we can honor Sylvia with a statue on campus, giving our fans a lasting symbol that celebrates her remarkable legacy."

Fowles' legacy stretches far past LSU's campus. Fowles was selected second overall in the 2008 WNBA Draft by the Chicago Sky . After joining the Minnesota Lynx in 2015, she helped lead the franchise to WNBA championships in 2015 and 2017, earning Finals MVP honors both times. She was named league MVP in 2017 and earned WNBA Defensive Player of the Year four times (2011, 2013, 2016, and 2021). Fowles was an eight-time WNBA All-Star and four-time Olympic gold medalist with Team USA.

Fowles joined the Portland Fire coaching staff in December as an assistant to head coach Alex Sarama.

articles.title: Mets pitcher Robert Stock done for season due to numbness in his fingers
articles.summary: Robert Stock’s comeback season ended Wednesday, when the New York Mets right-hander was placed on the 15-day injured list due to numbness in his fingers.  St...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Robert Stock 's comeback season ended Wednesday, when the New York Mets right-hander was placed on the 15-day injured list due to numbness in his fingers.

Stock had been scheduled to start the series finale Wednesday night against Pete Alonso and the Baltimore Orioles . Instead, right-hander Xzavion Curry was recalled from Triple-A Syracuse to make the start at Citi Field.

New York also put right-handed reliever Daniel Duarte on the 15-day IL with a left hamstring strain, ending his season. Left-hander Jefry Yan was recalled from Syracuse.

The 29-year-old Duarte went 2-0 with a 2.12 ERA and two saves in 24 appearances for the last-place Mets this season. He struck out 30 and walked seven in 29 2/3 innings.

Stock said his condition is a byproduct of the thoracic outlet syndrome surgery he underwent in March. He said he would usually begin to experience numbness after throwing about 60 or 70 pitches in a game.

The 36-year-old Stock, who has pitched for eight big league organizations as well as in Korea and for the independent Long Island Ducks, is on medication for the condition but said he didn't want to risk giving the Mets a short start after their bullpen accounted for 8 2/3 innings over the previous two games.

"It's not fair to the team for me to go out there and say, hey, is this going to work or not on a day when we really need our starting pitcher to go out there and do his job," Stock said.

Stock finished 1-3 with a 5.93 ERA in eight games (seven starts) for the Mets this season. The win was his first in the majors since 2019.

He called the experience a "dream come true" and said he hoped to be in the mix for a roster spot next year.

"I've proven that my name should be in the conversation for being a major league pitcher," Stock said. "Obviously, there's a million things that I want to improve upon and do better that will help me continue on."

articles.title: NCAA's FBS Oversight Committee finds replay error marred Western Michigan-Michigan game
articles.summary: Western Michigan got hosed during their season-opening game against Michigan, and everyone knows it.
articles.body:
Western Michigan got hosed during their season-opening game against Michigan, and everyone knows it.

The NCAA's FBS Oversight Committee knows it, too.

Via Nick Bromberg of Yahoo Sports, the NCAA released a statement on Wednesday acknowledging that the replay process reached the wrong result .

"The committee consulted with national officiating leadership regarding the instant replay protocols," the statement explained. "Based on that information, the committee agreed that the instant replay protocols were not followed in the contest's second-to-last play. Had the protocols been followed, the outcome of the game would have been different."

However, the committee also said that the rules do not prevent an appeal of the outcome of any game, once the game is declared to be ended.

While the statement won't change the official outcome, it reinforces the unofficial belief that Western Michigan won the game. Because Western Michigan did win the game.
